implementation_notes: Default realization: an integer lock_version column on the root record (and none on the members). Each save of the root emits an UPDATE guarded by the loaded version and raises ActiveRecord::StaleObjectError when someone else got there first; the exception is the application's cue to reload, merge or retry. One column on the root replaces per-member version columns, and the docs' recommended wiring is to carry the root's lock_version in the form so the check survives the request boundary.

variants.name: ActiveRecord lock_version on the root record
variants.implementation_notes: Default realization: an integer lock_version column on the root record (and none on the members). Each save of the root emits an UPDATE guarded by the loaded version and raises ActiveRecord::StaleObjectError when someone else got there first; the exception is the application's cue to reload, merge or retry. One column on the root replaces per-member version columns, and the docs' recommended wiring is to carry the root's lock_version in the form so the check survives the request boundary.
variants.code_sketch:
class Order < ApplicationRecord          # lock_version is a column
  has_many :lines
end

order = Order.find(id)
order.lines.build(qty: 3)                 # member change
begin
  order.save!                             # StaleObjectError if stale
rescue ActiveRecord::StaleObjectError
  order.reload                          # merge or retry
end
pitfalls: Saving a member directly (line.save!) never checks the root version, so the guard only holds if member changes go through the root's save or the root is always touched.
lock_optimistically = false and a custom locking_column are global/class switches - a forgotten rename silently drops the check.

variants.name: ActiveRecord lock!/with_lock on the root record
variants.implementation_notes: Pessimistic realization: reload the root under a row lock with record.lock! or wrap the whole edit in record.with_lock { ... }, which starts a transaction, reloads the record with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE and yields with the lock held (Model.lock.find(id) does the same for a query). The block form replaces lock bookkeeping entirely - the transaction releases the root lock on exit - and every member written inside the block is covered by it. Use it when the conflict is expensive enough to block other writers.
variants.code_sketch:
order = Order.find(id)
order.with_lock do
  # transaction + SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the root
  order.lines.each { |line| line.apply!(delta) }
  order.save!
end
# lock released when the block's transaction ends
pitfalls: lock! reloads the record and refuses to run when there are unsaved changes; save or discard first, or the call raises.
A custom locking clause (e.g. 'FOR UPDATE NOWAIT') is database-specific, and holding the lock across an external HTTP call turns the cluster lock into a latency amplifier.
